content: Koch's postulates, also known as Henle-Koch postulates, are a set of four criteria established to determine a causal relationship between a specific microorganism and a disease. These postulates were originally formulated by Robert Koch and Friedrich Loeffler in 1884, and later refined and published by Koch in 1890. Koch utilized these postulates to identify the causative agents of anthrax and tuberculosis, and they have since been applied to other diseases. The postulates are as follows: 1. The microorganism must be present in all individuals suffering from the disease and absent in healthy individuals. 2. The microorganism must be isolated from a diseased organism and grown in pure culture. 3. The cultured microorganism should cause the same disease when introduced into a healthy organism. 4. The microorganism must be re-isolated from the experimentally infected host and identified as identical to the original causative agent. However, Koch later abandoned the second part of the first postulate after discovering asymptomatic carriers of diseases such as cholera and, later, the infamous case of Typhoid Mary. It is now well-established that asymptomatic carriers are a common feature of many infectious diseases, particularly viral infections like polio, herpes simplex, HIV, and hepatitis C. For example, while poliovirus is known to cause paralysis in only a small percentage of infected individuals, the effectiveness of the polio vaccine in preventing disease strongly supports the conclusion that the poliovirus is the causative agent. The third postulate uses the term should rather than must because, as Koch himself demonstrated with tuberculosis and cholera, not all organisms exposed to an infectious agent will develop the disease. This variability can be attributed to factors such as chance, acquired immunity, or genetic immunity. An example of genetic immunity is the resistance to HIV infection observed in individuals carrying the CCR5-Δ32 deletion mutation. Koch's postulates were developed in the 19th century as general guidelines for identifying pathogens that could be isolated using the techniques available at the time. Even during Koch's era, it was recognized that some infectious agents were clearly responsible for disease despite not fulfilling all the postulates. Attempts to rigidly apply Koch's postulates to the diagnosis of viral diseases in the late 19th century, when viruses could not yet be visualized or cultured, may have hindered the early progress of virology as a field. Today, many infectious agents are accepted as causes of disease even though they do not meet all of Koch's postulates. As a result, while Koch's postulates remain historically significant and continue to inform microbiological diagnostic approaches, fulfilling all four postulates is no longer considered necessary to establish causality. Furthermore, Koch's postulates have influenced scientists studying microbial pathogenesis from a molecular perspective. In the 1980s, a molecular version of Koch's postulates was developed to guide the identification of microbial genes responsible for encoding virulence factors.
